```{python}
#| include: false
import json
import time
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown

from tsp_ga import Config, load, run

INK = "#1B1B19"
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": "white", "axes.facecolor": "white", "savefig.facecolor": "white",
    "text.color": INK, "axes.edgecolor": INK, "axes.labelcolor": INK,
    "xtick.color": INK, "ytick.color": INK, "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.linewidth": 0.6, "font.size": 10,
    "legend.frameon": False, "lines.color": INK, "axes.prop_cycle": plt.cycler(color=[INK]),
})
STYLES = ["-", "--", ":", "-."]

root = Path.cwd() if (Path.cwd() / "web").exists() else Path.cwd().parent
D = json.loads((root / "web" / "data" / "experiments.json").read_text())
SEEDS, BUDGET = D["seeds"], D["budget"]
pct = lambda v, d=0: f"{100 * v:.{d}f}%"
small = lambda v: f"{100 * v:.2f}%"
arm = lambda rows, name: next(r for r in rows if r["arm"] == name)
table = lambda df, **kw: Markdown(df.to_markdown(index=False, **kw))
signed = lambda c: f"{100 * c['difference']:+.1f} ({100 * c['lo']:+.1f} to {100 * c['hi']:+.1f})"

QA, DJ, ER = D["schedules"]["qa194"], D["schedules"]["dj38"], D["schedules_er"]["qa194"]
OPS = D["operators"]["qa194"]
MEM = {(m["instance"], m["budget"]): m for m in D["memetic"]}
MQ, MU = MEM[("qa194", BUDGET)], next(m for m in D["memetic"] if m["instance"] == "uy734")
F2020 = "Funnel 700 to 200 (2020)"
H = lambda stage, x: next(r for r in D["heritability"] if r["stage"] == stage and r["crossover"] == x)
```

## Summary

In 2020 I wrote a genetic algorithm for the travelling salesman problem and gave it an idea
borrowed from plant breeding: a *selection funnel*, a population that starts large and shrinks
every generation. I never tested whether it helped. This report does, and it also asks whether
the idea was new.

```{python}
#| echo: false
best_q = arm(QA["arms"], QA["verdict"]["best_fixed"])
best_m = arm(MQ["arms"], MQ["verdict"]["best_fixed"])
fun_m = arm(MQ["arms"], "Funnel 80 to 10")
Markdown(f"""
- **The funnel does little.** At the 2020 budget on Qatar (194 cities) the original program
  ends {pct(arm(QA['arms'], F2020)['gap'])} above the shortest tour. Against a fixed population
  of the same average size the difference is {signed(QA['verdict']['funnel_vs_same_average'])}
  percentage points. Choosing a better fixed size ({QA['verdict']['best_fixed'].lower()})
  gives {pct(best_q['gap'])}.
- **The operators matter far more.** Swapping the mutation for an inversion takes Qatar from
  {pct(arm(OPS, 'pmx+swap')['gap'])} to {pct(arm(OPS, 'pmx+inversion')['gap'])}; edge
  recombination with inversion reaches {pct(arm(OPS, 'er+inversion')['gap'])}.
- **Two breeding measurements explain why.** With partially mapped crossover, children of
  decent parents are {pct(H('After 100 generations', 'pmx')['load'])} longer than their
  parents, and the population ends {pct(D['traces']['arms'][0]['kinship'][-1])} inbred.
- **Cross, then refine.** Adding 2-opt local search to every child brings Qatar to
  {small(best_m['gap'])} of optimal at the same budget. Local search with no breeding stops
  at {small(MQ['restarts']['gap'])}.
- **With local search the funnel has a narrow use.** It is the best setting on Qatar at the
  full budget ({small(fun_m['gap'])}, optimal in {fun_m['solved'] * fun_m['n']:.0f} of
  {fun_m['n']} runs) and a poor one whenever work is scarce: on Uruguay (734 cities) it ends
  at {small(arm(MU['arms'], 'Funnel 80 to 10')['gap'])} against
  {small(arm(MU['arms'], MU['verdict']['best_fixed'])['gap'])} for a small fixed population.
- **None of it was new.** Breeding theory entered genetic algorithms in 1993, and shrinking
  the population linearly is a published, competition-winning technique from 2014.
""")
```

The [web page](../) runs the same algorithm in the browser.

## The problem and the test

A tour visits every city once and returns to the start. The instances are three of the
[national TSPs](https://www.math.uwaterloo.ca/tsp/world/countries.html) from the University of
Waterloo. Distances are Euclidean, rounded to the nearest whole number as TSPLIB specifies,
and the optimal tour of each is known. Every result is reported as a **gap**: how much longer
the tour is than the optimal one.

```{python}
#| echo: false
table(pd.DataFrame([{"Instance": v["title"], "Optimal tour": f"{v['optimum']:,}"} for v in D["instances"].values()]))
```

The algorithm keeps the best `s` tours each generation (truncation selection) and makes `s`
children. For each child, two survivors are picked at random and crossed both ways; each of
the two offspring is mutated with probability 0.15, and the shorter one is kept. The 2020
funnel sets `s = 200 + 500 (1 − g / 300)` in generation `g`.

**The budget.** Comparing methods by generations would be meaningless when the population
changes size. The unit here is the *tour evaluation*. The 2020 settings spend
`{python} f"{BUDGET:,}"` of them, and every method below gets exactly that. Local search is
charged too: checking one 2-opt move costs 4/*n* of an evaluation, since it reads four
distances where a full evaluation reads *n*. Runs stop when the budget is spent.

Every figure is the mean over `{python} SEEDS` seeds, with a 95% bootstrap interval. Comparisons are paired
by seed.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "One run of the 2020 settings"
qa = load("qa194")
run(qa, Config(), 1)  # compile
t = time.perf_counter()
r = run(qa, Config(), 1)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t
Markdown(f"Seed 1: tour of **{r.length:,}**, {pct(r.gap)} above the optimal {qa.optimum:,}, "
         f"in {elapsed:.2f} s. The 2020 script took 8.5 minutes for the same run.")
```

One correction to 2020: the original scored an open path, without the leg home, so its lengths
could not be compared with published optima. Its README reported 26,013 for Qatar; on closed
tours the same settings average `{python} f"{9352 * (1 + arm(QA['arms'], F2020)['gap']):,.0f}"`.
The rebuild reproduces the old program, flaw for flaw, before changing anything.

## Does the funnel help?

Three comparisons answer different questions: the funnel against a fixed population of its own
average size (does the *shape* matter?), against the best fixed size (would tuning one number
do better?), and against itself reversed (does the *direction* matter?).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Gap at the 2020 budget, partially mapped crossover and swap mutation. Line: fixed populations. Horizontal bars: funnels, spanning the sizes they pass through."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.6))
for ax, block, title in zip(axes, (QA, DJ), ("Qatar", "Djibouti")):
    fixed = [a for a in block["arms"] if a["schedule"] == "fixed"]
    x = [a["sizes"][0] for a in fixed]
    ax.plot(x, [100 * a["gap"] for a in fixed], "-s", ms=3, lw=1)
    ax.fill_between(x, [100 * a["lo"] for a in fixed], [100 * a["hi"] for a in fixed], color=INK, alpha=0.12, lw=0)
    for a, ls in zip([a for a in block["arms"] if a["schedule"] != "fixed"], STYLES):
        ax.plot(a["sizes"], [100 * a["gap"]] * 2, ls=ls, lw=2, marker="|", ms=7, label=a["arm"])
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("Tours kept each generation"); ax.set_ylabel("Gap (%)")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = []
for label, block in (("Qatar, 2020 operators", QA), ("Djibouti, 2020 operators", DJ), ("Qatar, edge recombination + inversion", ER)):
    v = block["verdict"]
    rows.append({"Setting": label, "2020 funnel": pct(arm(block["arms"], F2020)["gap"], 1),
                 "Best fixed size": f"{v['best_fixed'].replace('Fixed ', '')} ({pct(arm(block['arms'], v['best_fixed'])['gap'], 1)})",
                 "vs same average size": signed(v["funnel_vs_same_average"]),
                 "vs best fixed": signed(v["funnel_vs_best_fixed"]),
                 "vs reversed": signed(v["funnel_vs_reverse"])})
table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

Differences are in percentage points of gap, funnel minus the alternative, so negative favours
the funnel.

The shape has a small effect at most. On Qatar with the 2020 operators it is
indistinguishable from a fixed population of the same average size. On Djibouti, and on Qatar
with better operators, it beats that rival by five or six points, and it beats the reversed
funnel in two cases of three. So shrinking is, if anything, the right direction. But the best
fixed size beats the funnel by about fifty points on Qatar under either set of operators, and
the best size itself moves from 1,000 on Djibouti to 20–50 on Qatar. Population size is the
parameter that matters, and the funnel is one more way of not having tuned it.

## What does help

```{python}
#| echo: false
names = {"pmx": "Partially mapped (2020)", "ox": "Order", "er": "Edge recombination"}
rows = [{"Crossover": names[x], "Swap mutation (2020)": pct(arm(OPS, f"{x}+swap")["gap"], 1),
         "Inversion mutation": pct(arm(OPS, f"{x}+inversion")["gap"], 1)} for x in names]
table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

Qatar, fixed population of 100, same budget. Both changes are the same idea. A tour's length
is a sum over its **edges**, the roads between consecutive cities. Inversion reverses a stretch
of the tour and changes two edges. Swapping two cities changes four. Edge recombination builds
a child almost entirely from edges of its parents. Partially mapped crossover preserves the
*positions* of cities, which mean nothing in a round trip.

## A breeder's measurements

Here the breeding analogy earns its keep. Three quantities from quantitative genetics can be
measured on a genetic algorithm directly.

**Crossing cost.** Take a population, cross 5,000 random pairs with no mutation and no
selection, and compare offspring with the mean of their parents. A positive value means the
cross itself does damage, which selection must then repair.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = [{"Parents": f"{h['stage']} ({pct(h['parent_gap'])} gap)", "Crossover": names[h["crossover"]].replace(" (2020)", ""),
         "Parental edges inherited": pct(h["inherited"]), "Offspring longer than parents by": pct(h["load"], 1),
         "Offspring beating the better parent": pct(h["better_than_parents"], 1)}
        for h in D["heritability"] if h["stage"] != "Random tours"]
table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

Among random tours all three crossovers are harmless, because there is nothing to break. Once
the parents are any good, partially mapped crossover makes children
`{python} pct(H('After 30 generations', 'pmx')['load'])` to
`{python} pct(H('After 100 generations', 'pmx')['load'])` longer than their parents. About a
fifth of a child's edges are new and random, and a random edge across Qatar is many times
longer than a good one. Early in a run, one such cross in
`{python} f"{1 / H('After 30 generations', 'pmx')['better_than_parents']:.0f}"` beats its
better parent, against one in
`{python} f"{1 / H('After 30 generations', 'er')['better_than_parents']:.0f}"` for edge
recombination.

**Inbreeding.** The share of edges that the survivors have in common with the best tour.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Inbreeding over a run on Qatar with the 2020 funnel, by crossover. Mean of 20 runs."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
for t, ls in zip(D["traces"]["arms"][:3], STYLES):
    ax.plot(t["generation"], [100 * k for k in t["kinship"]], ls=ls, lw=1.2, label=t["arm"])
ax.set_xlabel("Generation"); ax.set_ylabel("Edges shared with the best tour (%)"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The two measurements are one story. When nearly every cross between different parents fails,
the only offspring that survive truncation are those of near-identical parents, which are
near-copies. The population collapses onto its best member and the algorithm degenerates into
a slow mutation-only search. This also explains why small populations did best with the 2020
operators: if crossover contributes nothing, more generations of mutation is the better use of
the budget.

A caution on the third quantity. I also estimated heritability by regressing offspring length
on mid-parent length. It comes out high for all three crossovers (0.7 and above), including the
one that fails, because a child of long parents is long whatever else happens. In this setting
heritability does not separate good operators from bad ones; crossing cost does. The same
point was made, in different terms, by
Manderick, de Weger and Spiessens (1991),
who used parent–offspring fitness correlation to rank operators.

## Cross, then refine

The breeding funnel I copied in 2020 does not describe a population that shrinks while it
keeps interbreeding. A pedigree programme makes its crosses once, and then spends years
selecting within the progeny and fixing them, with cheap tests on the many early on and
expensive trials on the few at the end. The nearest thing in an optimiser is to follow each
cross with refinement of the offspring: a *memetic algorithm*. Here the refinement is 2-opt
with neighbour lists (try reconnecting each city to one of its eight nearest neighbours; keep
any change that shortens the tour; repeat until none does).

```{python}
#| echo: false
def mem_table(block):
    names = ["Fixed 5", "Fixed 10", "Fixed 20", "Fixed 40", "Fixed 80", "Funnel 80 to 10",
             "Steep funnel 200 to 5", "Steep funnel, effort 1 to full", "Fixed 20, partially mapped", "Fixed 20, order"]
    rows = [arm(block["arms"], n) for n in names] + [block["restarts"]]
    return table(pd.DataFrame([{"Population": a["arm"], "Gap": small(a["gap"]),
                                "95% interval": f"{small(a['lo'])} to {small(a['hi'])}",
                                "Optimal runs": f"{a['solved'] * a['n']:.0f} of {a['n']}"} for a in rows]))
Markdown(f"**Qatar, {BUDGET:,} evaluations.** Edge recombination and inversion unless stated.")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
mem_table(MQ)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
Markdown(f"**Uruguay, 734 cities, same budget.**")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
mem_table(MU)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Qatar with local search: gap against the work allowed."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
qs = sorted((m for m in D["memetic"] if m["instance"] == "qa194"), key=lambda m: m["budget"])
bx = [m["budget"] for m in qs]
for name, ls in zip(["Fixed 10", "Fixed 40", "Funnel 80 to 10"], STYLES):
    ax.plot(bx, [100 * arm(m["arms"], name)["gap"] for m in qs], ls=ls, lw=1.2, marker="s", ms=3, label=name)
ax.plot(bx, [100 * m["restarts"]["gap"] for m in qs], ls=STYLES[3], lw=1.2, marker="s", ms=3, label="No breeding")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("Tour evaluations allowed"); ax.set_ylabel("Gap (%)"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Four things follow.

1. Local search is worth more than every other change put together, and it is not doing the
   work alone: 2-opt from random starts, with no breeding, is more than ten times further from
   optimal at the full budget.
2. With local search the choice of crossover nearly stops mattering. Refinement repairs the
   damage of a bad cross.
3. The funnel becomes the best setting on Qatar at the full budget, though its advantage over
   the best fixed population
   (`{python} signed(MQ['verdict']['best_funnel_vs_best_fixed'])` points) is within noise. At
   a quarter or a sixteenth of the budget, and on Uruguay, where the same budget is spread
   over 734 cities, it is clearly worse than a small fixed population. A wide start pays only
   when there is work to spare.
4. The other half of the breeder's funnel, cheap screening early and thorough refinement late
   ("effort 1 to full"), was never the best setting.

## Was it original?

No. I did not know the literature in 2020; this is what it already contained.

| Idea in the 2020 project | Prior work |
|---|---|
| Apply breeding practice to a genetic algorithm | Mühlenbein and Schlierkamp-Voosen, [Predictive models for the Breeder Genetic Algorithm](https://doi.org/10.1162/evco.1993.1.1.25), *Evolutionary Computation* 1(1), 1993. Truncation selection, the breeder's equation, response to selection and heritability. |
| A population whose size changes during the run | Arabas, Michalewicz and Mulawka, GAVaPS: a genetic algorithm with varying population size, *IEEE ICEC* 1994, pp. 73–78. |
| Shrinking it linearly | Tanabe and Fukunaga, Improving the search performance of SHADE using linear population size reduction, *IEEE CEC* 2014, pp. 1658–1665 (L-SHADE, winner of the CEC 2014 competition). |
| Operators judged by parent–offspring resemblance | Manderick, de Weger and Spiessens, The genetic algorithm and the structure of the fitness landscape, *ICGA* 1991, pp. 143–150. |
| Crossover followed by local search | Memetic algorithms, from Moscato (1989); for the TSP, edge-preserving crossover with local search is the basis of the strongest evolutionary solvers. |

The funnel's other half, cheap evaluation for many candidates and careful evaluation for a
few survivors, is the principle of successive halving and Hyperband in hyperparameter search.
That is where the breeding funnel is at home, because there, as in a field trial, evaluating a
candidate properly is expensive and a rough evaluation is informative. A tour's length is exact
and cheap, so there is nothing for the funnel to economise on.

What I would defend from the original is the instinct, not the mechanism. Breeders measure
what their crosses do. Crossing cost and inbreeding, measured on the 2020 program, diagnose it
in two numbers.

## Limits

- Three instances, of 38, 194 and 734 cities, and one budget with two smaller ones on Qatar.
  The conclusions about population size in particular are budget-dependent, as the Uruguay
  result shows.
- Mutation probability stayed at the 2020 value of 0.15 and selection stayed truncation. A
  funnel might interact with either.
- Funnels were compared at a few shapes, not optimised. Neither were the fixed populations
  beyond a grid of sizes.
- This is a study of an idea, not a competitive solver. Concorde solves all three instances
  to optimality; Lin–Kernighan-style local search would beat 2-opt.
- Intervals are bootstrap intervals over `{python} SEEDS` seeds and are not corrected for the number of
  comparisons.

## Reproducing this

```bash
uv sync --group report
uv run pytest
uv run tsp-ga build        # every experiment; writes web/data/experiments.json
npm test                   # includes the Python-to-JavaScript parity test
QUARTO_PYTHON=.venv/bin/python quarto render report/index.qmd
```

Random numbers come from a counter-based generator (MurmurHash3's 32-bit finaliser applied to
seed, stream and counter), implemented identically in Python and JavaScript, so a seed
identifies a run in both.
